# What a Negative Prompt Is and When to Use One in AI Image Tools

> **In short:** A negative prompt tells an AI image or video generator what to leave out, such as logos, text or stray people. According to PIXLR, it lets you fix one flaw without rewriting the parts of your picture that already work.

Have you ever generated a picture that was almost perfect, then spotted a sixth finger, a made-up logo on a product or a stranger in the back of a listing photo? That's the moment a negative prompt is useful.

## The basic idea

A prompt (the instruction you type to an AI tool) usually describes what you want. A negative prompt describes what you don't want. Think of it as a "please avoid" list that sits next to your main request.

There's one nuance to keep in mind. A negative prompt doesn't delete anything. It nudges the generator away from the items you listed. PIXLR describes it as guidance rather than a guarantee, so you should still check each result.

## Why it saves time

Without a negative prompt, the usual cycle goes like this: generate, notice a problem, reword the prompt, generate again, and often end up with a different picture than the one you liked. Each attempt can use up credits (the units many tools use to measure how much you've generated).

A short, targeted negative term lets you keep the composition you like and subtract only the flaw. PIXLR also points out that some defects make an image unusable for real work. A logo on a product or a person in a property listing can be a deal-breaker, and a few well-chosen exclusions can be the difference between "almost right" and "ready to use."

## Terms to start with

PIXLR's guide groups common exclusions by goal. Here are a few examples:

- **General quality**: text, watermark, logo, signature, blurry, low resolution
- **People**: bad anatomy, extra fingers, missing fingers, deformed
- **Clean backgrounds**: people, background clutter, power lines, trash, reflections
- **Video**: flickering, morphing, warping, text shifting, floating objects

You don't need all of them every time. Pick the handful that match your goal.

## Simple rules to follow

- **Be specific.** "Blurry, low contrast" gives the tool more to work with than "bad quality."
- **Keep the list short.** A few targeted terms usually work better than a long list.
- **Fix what you see.** Generate first, then add a term for the problem that actually showed up.
- **Write plain terms.** The negative field already means "avoid these," so you don't need to add extra wording to each item.
- **Keep your positive anchors.** If you want natural-looking skin, say so in the main prompt too.

Availability can vary, too. PIXLR notes that its image and video generators support negative prompts depending on the AI model you pick.

## Two quick examples

PIXLR gives two examples that show the idea well. In the first, a product-style shot needs to be free of third-party brands, logos and landmarks to avoid copyright trouble, so those items go in the negative prompt. In the second, a café portrait stays focused on the woman at the table, and the negative prompt excludes other people in the background.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you make cards, wallpapers or hobby art, add one exclusion for whatever keeps bothering you, such as text or watermarks.
- **For your business or work**: If you sell products or list homes, keep a standard set of exclusions for logos, people and clutter so your images are ready to publish sooner.
- **If you're just getting started**: Generate one image without a negative prompt, write down the flaw you notice, and add one matching term next time.
- **If you already use it**: For video, pair a short list of stability terms, such as flickering and morphing, with a clear description of the motion you want in the main prompt.

## Wrap-up

A negative prompt is a simple list of things to avoid, and it works best when it's short, specific and aimed at a problem you've actually seen. Try it on your next image: generate once, note the one flaw that bothers you, and add a single term to fix it. You'll learn quickly which exclusions your favorite tool responds to.
